extracted.intended_audience: NIH R01 applicants (especially new/early-stage investigators), grant applicants and mentors
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding criteria and evaluative dimensions used by NIH study sections to review R01 research grant applications (Significance, Investigator(s), Innovation, Approach, Environment), plus related administrative and policy considerations (human subjects, animals, resource sharing, budget, new investigator policies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgement of the application’s likely overall influence on the field; reviewers provide an overall impact score (1-9) reflecting their assessment of the likelihood that the project will exert a sustained, powerful influence on the research field(s) involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall impact is based on discussion and the reviewers’ averaged overall scores, then multiplied by 10 to produce the impact/priority score. It reflects the combined consideration of the criterion scores (Significance, Investigator(s), Innovation, Approach, Environment) and the summary discussion; criterion scores are submitted prior to the meeting and are not individually discussed. Review text shows how strengths and weaknesses across criteria (e.g., significance, innovation, feasibility) are weighed to justify the overall impact. Reviewers enumerate both strengths and weaknesses and note whether weaknesses materially affect impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the project addresses an important problem or critical barrier to progress in the field and will advance scientific knowledge or clinical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers consider relevance to human disease/public health, potential to shift paradigms, ability to fill knowledge gaps, and applicability to other systems. Example strengths: tractable model system, applicability to other viruses, paradigm-shifting preliminary data implicating novel factors (e.g., mismatch repair proteins), and potential to identify therapeutic targets. Weaknesses should be noted if the problem is of limited scope or of lesser public health importance. Reviewers explicitly list strengths (how findings extend the field) and absence of weaknesses when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the PI(s) and team’s qualifications, productivity, and suitability to carry out the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider PI training, publication record, relevant technical expertise, prior discoveries that underpin the proposal, and strength of collaborators/co-investigators. Reviewers cite concrete evidence (e.g., prior work on BKPyV, specific technical experience like 2-D gels/DNA fiber assays). For new investigators, reviewers note institutional support and mentorship. Weaknesses are noted when qualifications, experience, or the team composition raise concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of whether the application challenges and seeks to shift current research or clinical practice paradigms using novel concepts, methods, or interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers look for conceptual novelty (e.g., hypothesis that viral replication—not only viral protein—triggers DDR), use of cutting-edge techniques (iPOND, SILAC, 2-D LC-MS/MS), and biologically relevant models (primary RPTE cells). Strengths and novelty are enumerated; lack of innovation is cited as a weakness. Innovation can be incremental if combined with novel application or synthesis of methods to address new questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the overall strategy, experimental design, methods, analyses, feasibility, and consideration of potential problems and alternative approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers examine clarity and logic of aims, adequacy of preliminary data, experimental controls, statistical considerations (biological vs technical replicates), feasibility of state-of-the-art methods (and whether feasibility data are provided), and whether alternative strategies are proposed if initial approaches fail. Strengths include well-described, testable aims, appropriate controls, and discussion of outcomes that would disprove hypotheses along with alternative experiments. Weaknesses include missing feasibility data for specialized techniques, unclear rationale for specific reagents/constructs, modest effect sizes requiring multiple biological replicates, or insufficient detail in some aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of institutional support, availability of resources, facilities, and whether the scientific environment will contribute to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers consider departmental/institutional commitment (e.g., strong chair letter), core facilities, collaborative support, and environment for trainee/PI success. Strengths include outstanding physical and scientific environment and documented institutional commitment. Weaknesses are noted if environment/resources are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections for Human Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether human subjects protections are appropriately addressed and applicable human subjects issues (if any) are managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications involving human subjects, reviewers assess protections, risk minimization, and consent. In this application the entry is 'Not Applicable (No Human Subjects)'. When applicable, reviewers will list protections and deficiencies; absence of required protections is a significant concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebrate Animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the proposed use of live vertebrate animals and whether vertebrate animal protections and justifications are adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers check for justification of animal use, appropriateness of species and numbers, and animal welfare protections. In this application the entry is 'Not Applicable (No Vertebrate Animals)'. If applicable, strengths/weaknesses in animal plans are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biohazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of potential biohazard risks and whether biosafety plans and facilities are adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers note whether proposed work involves biohazards and if appropriate biosafety measures and approvals are in place. This application marked 'Not Applicable (No Biohazards)' in some critiques and 'Acceptable' later where BSL-2 work is noted with training, designated areas, audits, and occupational health protections. Deficiencies in biosafety plans are raised as weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select Agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether any select agents are involved and whether appropriate compliance measures are described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must disclose select agent use and provide requisite approvals and containment plans. In this application the entry is 'Not Applicable (No Select Agents)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource Sharing Plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether plans for sharing relevant research resources (data, reagents, models) are adequate and acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers evaluate existence and adequacy of resource sharing plans. In this application the plan is judged 'Unacceptable' and noted as a deficiency. A clear, acceptable resource sharing plan is expected and lack thereof can be raised as a serious concern in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and Period of Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the requested budget and proposed period of support for appropriateness and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers (and grants management) judge if the budget is reasonable and justified; the committee can recommend as requested or recommend adjustments. Here the recommendation was 'Recommend as Requested'. Administrative notes clarify that the requested budget may be adjusted by grants management if an award is planned and that committee recommendations inform grant management calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Health Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement of how the proposed research is relevant to public health and disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers expect an explicit public health relevance statement describing potential impact (e.g., revealing therapeutic host targets, implications for polyomavirus-related diseases). This section helps reviewers and program staff assess broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: New/Early Stage Investigator Policies and Resubmission Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Special NIH considerations for new investigators (early stage/new investigator R01 resubmission policies and opportunities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH policy affords special practices for new investigators (e.g., special receipt dates and expedited resubmission opportunities). The summary advises contacting the program officer about fundability and resubmission timing; it provides a firm resubmission receipt deadline (e.g., amended application must be received by Dec 10, 2015 for expedited consideration) and references Guide Notices (NOT-OD-11-057, NOT-OD-14-074). Applicants are advised to seek mentor/departmental input when revising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring Procedure and Percentile / Impact Score Calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative rules governing how criterion and overall scores are collected and converted to impact/priority scores and percentiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion scores are submitted by individual reviewers prior to the meeting and are not discussed at the meeting. The overall impact score is calculated by averaging all voting reviewers' overall scores (1-9) and multiplying by 10. Some applications also receive a percentile ranking. The summary notes recalibration efforts to address score inflation and establish percentile benchmarks for future meetings.
